text: This chapter has covered how to fine-tune a model. This closing lesson covers the failure mode that can undo all of it: a model that gets better at the task it was just fine-tuned on while getting measurably worse at everything it could already do before.

Gradient descent has no mechanism protecting old capabilities — it only reduces loss on whatever data is in front of it right now. So task-specific metrics go up while general-capability benchmarks the model was never fine-tuned on quietly go down. A team watching only their target metric can completely miss this.

Three things make it worse: a learning rate that's too high, meaning bigger overwrites per step; too many epochs over a small dataset, meaning repeated exposure with no counterbalancing diversity; and a training set that's narrow in topic relative to the model's original distribution. All three are exactly what a well-intentioned narrow fine-tune tends to create.

The most direct lever is simple: keep the learning rate modest relative to pretraining peak rates, and cap epochs — two to four is a common ceiling before forgetting risk rises sharply. Mixing in general-purpose data alongside the task-specific set helps too. And parameter-efficient methods like LoRA add a structural layer of protection, since the frozen base weights can't be overwritten at all — only the small adapter shifts.

Always evaluate a fine-tune on general capability, not just the target task, against the pre-fine-tuning checkpoint. That closes Chapter 4 — SFT gives you a model that follows instructions; what comes next is teaching it to prefer better answers over worse ones.
